title: VCSP tractability over the countable random graph
formal:
Let \(\mathbb R=(D;E)\) be the countable random graph. Is it true that for every valued structure \(\mathcal A=(D;f_1,\ldots,f_s)\) with a finite signature and \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb R)\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal A)\),
\[
\mathcal A\text{ does not pp-construct }K_3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{VCSP}(\mathcal A)\in\mathsf P?
\]
All cost functions take values in \(\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}\). The valued decision problem and the precise pp-construction condition are defined below. The template \(\mathcal A\) is fixed for each decision problem; the claim is not a uniform algorithm taking arbitrary templates as part of its input.
why: This asks whether the known expressibility obstruction completely determines tractability for a major new class of infinite-domain optimization problems. A positive answer would extend the algebraic classification of valued CSPs beyond ordered domains to graph-invariant costs; a counterexample would expose a failure of the proposed general obstruction.
status_note: Question 44 of the complete MFCS 2025 paper, repeated as Question 59 in arXiv:2409.07285v2 dated 20 January 2026, explicitly poses this random-graph tractability implication. sentences: The question concerns valued constraint problems whose costs depend only on equality and adjacency patterns in the countable random graph.
It asks whether every fixed finite-signature template is polynomial-time solvable whenever it cannot pp-construct a triangle.
The expressive closure includes sums, projection, scaling, feasibility and optimality, and the construction can use arbitrary finite powers.
The temporal classification proves an analogous result for ordered rationals but the January 2026 source still poses the random-graph case.
An accepted answer proves the full implication or an unconditional counterexample with its complexity lower bound in Lean.

definitions:
The countable random graph \(\mathbb R=(D;E)\), also called the Rado graph, is the countably infinite simple undirected graph with the extension property: for any disjoint finite sets \(U,V\subseteq D\), there is a vertex outside \(U\cup V\) adjacent to every vertex in \(U\) and to no vertex in \(V\). This property determines the graph up to isomorphism. The symbol \(\mathbb R\) denotes this graph here, not the real-number field. Its automorphisms are bijections \(\alpha:D\to D\) preserving adjacency and nonadjacency. No random graph is sampled in the algorithmic input.

A valued template consists of finitely many symbols \(f_i\), each with a fixed nonnegative finite arity \(k_i\), interpreted as \(f_i:D^{k_i}\to\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}\). The automorphism requirement says that \(f_i(\alpha(a_1),\ldots,\alpha(a_{k_i}))=f_i(a_1,\ldots,a_{k_i})\) for every automorphism \(\alpha\) of the graph and every tuple. Equivalently, a cost depends only on the equality pattern of its arguments and the adjacency pattern between their distinct entries. There are finitely many such patterns at each fixed arity, so each cost has a finite table of rational values and possible infinities. Negative rational costs are permitted. There are no distinguished domain constants or input vertex names.

For fixed \(\mathcal A\), an instance of \(\operatorname{VCSP}(\mathcal A)\) is an explicit finite set of variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\), a sum \(\Phi\) of atomic costs applied to these variables, and a rational threshold \(u\). An atomic cost is \(f_i(x_{j_1},\ldots,x_{j_{k_i}})\), the equality cost \(\operatorname{eq}(x,y)\) which is zero for equal arguments and infinity otherwise, or the always-infinite unary cost \(\bot(x)\). Variables may repeat within an atom, and atoms may repeat in the sum. The empty sum has value zero. Summands are explicitly listed with unit multiplicity; there are no binary-encoded external weights multiplying atoms. The question is whether there exists an assignment \(h:\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\to D\) with \(\Phi(h)\leq u\). Any infinite summand makes the sum infinite.

Encode the variable list explicitly, the sum as symbols with binary variable indices, and \(u\) by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. Let \(L\) be the total length. The template’s finite tables are fixed and may be built into a machine. Membership in \(\mathsf P\) means that some uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine decides this threshold language correctly on every valid input in at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit operations for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Malformed encodings are rejected. There is no randomness, numerical error, advice or oracle access to the infinite graph. The machine and its constants may depend on \(\mathcal A\); a common exponent, a template-classification algorithm and an assignment-output algorithm are not additionally required.

Here is an explicit equivalent form of the source’s valued pp-construction criterion. First define the valued relational clone \(\langle\mathcal A\rangle\): the smallest collection of finite-arity functions on \(D\) containing the template costs, equality and the always-infinite unary cost, and closed under the following operations. One may form finite sums of functions applied to variables with any repetitions, identifications or permutations, including the zero empty sum; add a rational constant; multiply by a nonnegative rational; or project by
\[
g(\mathbf a)=\inf_{\mathbf b\in D^r} f(\mathbf a,\mathbf b).
\]
Use \(0\cdot\infty=0\), \(c\cdot\infty=\infty\) for \(c>0\), and \(c+\infty=\infty\). Only functions valued in \(\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}\) are allowed. In this invariant setting every function produced has finitely many orbit values, so these projection infima are attained and remain rational or infinite.

Two further closure operations turn a function \(f\) into a crisp cost, meaning a function taking only zero and infinity. The feasibility cost is zero on \(\operatorname{Feas}(f)=\{\mathbf a:f(\mathbf a)<\infty\}\) and infinity outside it. The optimality cost is zero on
\[
\operatorname{Opt}(f)=\{\mathbf a:f(\mathbf a)<\infty\text{ and } f(\mathbf a)\leq f(\mathbf b)\text{ for every }\mathbf b\},
\]
and infinity outside it. If no tuple has finite cost, both sets are empty. The feasibility and optimality operations are part of the definition; using only sums and projection would give a different expressive closure. Membership in the clone requires a finite expression using these operations; arbitrary limits are not added.

Let \(K_3\) have vertices \(\{1,2,3\}\) and the binary adjacency relation consisting of all ordered pairs of distinct vertices. The template pp-constructs \(K_3\) precisely when there exist a positive integer \(d\), a crisp cost \(r\in\langle\mathcal A\rangle\) of arity \(2d\), and functions
\[
h:D^d\to\{1,2,3\},\qquad g:\{1,2,3\}\to D^d
\]
with the following properties. Define the binary relation \(H\) on \(D^d\) by \(H(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\) if and only if \(r(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=0\). Whenever \(H(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\), require \(h(\mathbf a)\ne h(\mathbf b)\); and whenever \(i\ne j\), require \(H(g(i),g(j))\). These are homomorphisms in both directions between \((D^d;H)\) and \(K_3\). The functions need not be computable or definable, and \(H\) need not be assumed symmetric in advance. This criterion includes arbitrary finite dimension and arbitrary expressible crisp costs, not only one graph relation from the original signature. Its equivalence with the source’s definition using valued pp-powers and fractional homomorphisms follows from Proposition 25 and the crisp homomorphism lemma in the full version.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its negation. A positive answer must prove polynomial-time decidability for every invariant finite-signature template that has no pp-construction of \(K_3\), under the full cost and input model above. The algorithm may depend on the fixed template, as membership of its language in \(\mathsf P\) permits.

A negative answer must establish a qualifying fixed template with no such pp-construction and prove that its threshold language is not in \(\mathsf P\). Merely proving NP-hardness gives a conditional counterexample under \(\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}\), not an unconditional refutation of the implication. A dichotomy without the specified pp-construction condition, a result only for temporal templates, or a result only for crisp or nonnegative finite-valued costs does not by itself settle this target. No decision procedure for recognizing the tractable templates is required beyond the source’s per-template assertion.

source_formulation.text: For every finite-signature valued structure preserved by all automorphisms of the countable random graph, does the absence of a pp-construction of K3 imply polynomial-time solvability of its VCSP?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the second part of Question 44, with the hypotheses supplied by its preceding sentence; repeated as Question 59 in the January 2026 full version.

context_blocks.text: The short imported question omitted the ambient class stated immediately before it. The countable random graph supplies that class: all costs are invariant under its automorphisms. Restoring this condition recovers the source’s exact scope. Arbitrary infinite-domain valued problems need not share the same tractability behavior.

Despite the infinite domain, every instance has a finite witness format for NP membership. Guess which variables are equal and the adjacency relation among their distinct assigned values. Every resulting finite simple graph embeds into the Rado graph by the extension property. The fixed pattern table evaluates every atomic cost, and exact rational arithmetic checks the threshold. This places each template’s language in NP without treating infinite-domain assignments as input strings or oracle answers.

The source’s pp-construction notion identifies a general reduction mechanism. Expressible costs can be implemented without changing polynomial-time solvability, finite powers encode tuples of domain elements, and homomorphisms transfer feasibility. Constructing the triangle in this way gives NP-hardness of the valued problem. The question asks whether absence of that obstruction always supplies tractability in this particular invariant class.

Feasibility alone discards relative preferences between assignments, while optimality singles out the tuples of minimum finite cost. Their separate presence in the expressive closure matters for the valued hardness criterion. The equivalent crisp construction above uses all crisp relations obtainable from the costs, not merely the feasibility relations of the originally supplied functions.

The temporal theorem concerns cost functions on the rationals invariant under every order-preserving bijection. It proves the corresponding polynomial-time versus NP-complete classification for that class, including the pp-construction criterion. The group of automorphisms of the countable random graph describes a different class, so the temporal theorem motivates the question but does not answer it.

The original Question 44 asks first for a complexity dichotomy and then for this sharper tractability implication. The imported card selects the second question. Combining its positive answer with the known hardness direction and the finite-pattern NP witness would give the broader dichotomy, while merely establishing a dichotomy would not identify its tractable side by this exact criterion.

In the general framework, the authors formulate a related conjecture for valued templates associated with reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. The random graph is a concrete highly symmetric test case. The January 2026 full version still explicitly poses this case after proving the temporal classification.
